To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

adversarially corrupted labels can be used to attack SVM classifiers, and that the attack is effective even in the presence of a significant amount of noise that does not affect the classifier performance.

adversarial label noise is a realistic threat to SVMs, that SVMs trained under label noise are more robust than their counterparts trained under benign noise, and that the noise rate is not the only parameter that matters, but also the noise distribution.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of adversarial label noise on Support Vector Machines, and how these effects can be mitigated by suitable modifications of the learning procedure.
the problem of learning a linear SVM in a setting in which the label information provided by the training set may be corrupted by an attacker.

the following question: Can we design a classifier which, when given a set of data points and a classifier, will output an adversarially modified set of labels which will maximize the classifier’s error?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the presence of label noise, SVMs are more robust to adversarial noise than NNs, and the latter are more robust to random noise.
SVM is the best classifier for binary classification tasks.
SVM is the best classification algorithm in most of the cases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show how adversarial examples are related to label noise.
we have developed a novel method for training Support Vector Machines under adversarial label noise.
we study the effects of adversarial label noise on the training performance of SVM classifiers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adversarial noise is not only a problem for deep learning, but also for SVMs.
the adversarial label noise problem is not just a theoretical problem.
adversarial label noise is a very serious problem for SVMs and can lead to a catastrophic performance drop, even when the noise is very sparse (i.e., only a few percent of the labels are flipped).
